newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Papua says U.N. should monitor French Pacific isles.
newsitem.headline: Papua says U.N. should monitor French Pacific isles.

text.p: The prime minister of Papua New Guinea suggested on Monday that French Polynesia, which includes Tahiti and is regarded as an integral part of France, should be listed by the United Nations as a non-self-governing territory.
The powers which administer such territories are obliged to submit periodic reports to the United Nations.

In a speech to the General Assembly, Sir Julius Chan said: "Having reviewed the French government's record elsewhere in the region, we ask ourselves whether French Polynesia as well as Wallis and Futuna should be included in the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories."

Chan, whose country has been strongly critical of now-finished French nuclear tests in the South Pacific, said the international community had a duty to "see that France meets its responsibilities to the people of our region. And a prime responsibility must be the right to self-determination."
He welcomed the end of French nuclear testing last year and the signing by Britain, France and the United States of the South Pacific nuclear free-zone treaty, known as the Treaty of Rarotonga.
But he said more was required before the region could be described as genuinely nuclear-free.

"Outstanding needs include a broader treaty, systematic monitoring of former test-sites, cleaning up, compensation -- and the provision of alternative sources of income for the people of French Polynesia," he said.
Replying at the end of the day, the secretary-general of the French delegation, Anne Gazeau-Secret, objected to Chan's comments about French Polynesia.
"The populations of these territories have continued to manifest in the most democratic way possible the fact that they are part of the French Republic," she said.
"The questions raised by the prime minister of Papua New Guinea are therefore, from the point of view of my delegation, pointless," she concluded.
